[Supreme Court]{.status .status-case} [420 U.S. 35](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-420/pdf/USREPORTS-420-35.pdf){.cite} [Decided February 18, 1975]{.cite} [9 to 0]{.cite}
:::

**Holding.** No. The statute required the Administrator to allot the full sums authorized; he had no discretion to withhold them. The Court decided the case on the statute alone and did not reach the constitutional question.

**Question.** Whether the Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency, at President Nixon's direction, could allot to the states less than the full amounts authorized for sewage treatment grants under the Federal Water Pollution Control Act Amendments of 1972.

Background reading: [Wikipedia article on Train v. New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Train_v._City_of_New_York) (secondary source).

## Why it matters

The Supreme Court's only decision on the Nixon impoundments. It shows how courts approach a refusal to spend: as a question of what the spending statute requires, not of inherent presidential power. That framing carries into disputes under the [Impoundment Control Act](../statutes/impoundment-1974.qmd), which gives the Comptroller General a statutory right to sue.

## How Congress responded

Congress had already acted: the [Impoundment Control Act](../statutes/impoundment-1974.qmd) was enacted in July 1974, while the case was pending.

## Status

Good law.

## Statutes at issue

- [Impoundment Control Act](../statutes/impoundment-1974.qmd){.subj}. Decided under the earlier water pollution statute, the case is the judicial counterpart to the act Congress passed while it was pending.

Studied in [Unit 4: The power of the purse](../study/units/purse.qmd).
